items.title: Rogers' Core Conditions
items.content: **Rogers' six-condition theory:** The two people are in psychological contact; the client is incongruent or vulnerable; the therapist is congruent; the therapist experiences unconditional positive regard and empathic understanding; and the client perceives at least some of that regard and empathy. Empathy, positive regard, and congruence are the three commonly emphasized therapist attitudes, not the complete six conditions or a guaranteed recipe for change.

items.title: Stages of Change (Transtheoretical)
items.content: **Behavior-specific readiness:** Precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance describe status with respect to a specified behavior; some accounts also discuss termination. Precontemplation does not necessarily mean no awareness, movement can be nonlinear, and relapse does not erase learning. Stage assessment and stage-matched support are hypotheses to evaluate, not rules that prohibit useful interventions or determine what a client must do.

items.title: Therapy Founders Quick Reference
items.content: **Historical orientation map:** Freud is associated with psychoanalysis; Skinner with radical behaviorism; Rogers with person-centered therapy; Beck with cognitive therapy; Ellis with REBT; Perls with Gestalt therapy; Linehan with DBT; Hayes and colleagues with ACT. Traditions evolved through many contributors, borrow techniques, and have different evidence bases. A founder-name cue cannot identify treatment from one technique or select care for a diagnosis.

items.title: Systematic Desensitization
items.content: **Historical graduated exposure procedure:** Systematic desensitization combines a collaboratively developed fear hierarchy with relaxation or another response while approaching feared material gradually, often imaginally. Anxiety and relaxation are not logically impossible together, and contemporary exposure accounts also emphasize expectancy change, inhibitory learning, tolerable engagement, and reduced avoidance. Flooding versus gradual and imaginal versus in-vivo are separate dimensions. Exposure requires consent, formulation, competence, and safety planning.

items.title: Ellis REBT - ABCDE Model
items.content: **REBT formulation:** A is an activating event, B the person's beliefs or evaluations, C emotional and behavioral consequences, D active disputation or examination, and E a more effective philosophy. The model emphasizes rigid demandingness, awfulizing, frustration intolerance, and global self or other rating. Events and beliefs interact with context; disputation is collaborative and not merely arguing. REBT is not uniformly confrontational, and a mnemonic does not select treatment.

items.title: DBT Skills - Linehan
items.content: **Four DBT skills modules:** Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness are taught within a comprehensive treatment that also uses behavioral assessment, target hierarchy, individual therapy, consultation, and between-session coaching in many programs. A skill acronym is not the whole treatment. Crisis-survival skills do not replace emergency care, and DBT selection and adaptation require qualified assessment, consent, culture, access, and outcome monitoring.

items.title: Gestalt Therapy Techniques
items.content: **Gestalt experiments:** Present-centered awareness, phenomenological inquiry, dialogue, empty-chair work, exaggeration, and attention to contact can be used as collaborative experiments. Empty-chair work does not mechanically resolve unfinished business, awareness alone is not guaranteed to cure, and slogans about responsibility can become blaming if detached from context. Technique choice depends on consent, relationship, formulation, stability, culture, competence, and the client's moment-to-moment response.

items.title: Solution-Focused Brief Therapy
items.content: **SFBT conversation practices:** Preferred-future or miracle questions clarify observable goals; exception questions explore times the concern is absent or less intense; scaling questions support description of position, resources, and next steps. The approach collaborates with the client's language and strengths, but does not assume every client already has a complete solution or that causes, trauma, safety, diagnosis, and structural constraints are irrelevant. Questions are adapted rather than scripted.

items.title: Family Therapy Models
items.content: **Model distinctions:** Structural therapy examines boundaries, subsystems, and hierarchy; Bowen theory emphasizes differentiation and multigenerational processes; strategic approaches use directives and interactional formulations; experiential approaches emphasize emotion, communication, and encounter. Models overlap and evolved through many contributors. A family pattern is not proof that a family caused an individual's symptoms, and assessment must include individual welfare, safety, coercion, culture, development, and context.

items.title: Group Therapy Stages
items.content: **Group development and therapeutic factors:** Forming, storming, norming, performing, and later adjourning are a heuristic sequence, not an invariant timetable. Yalom and Leszcz describe factors including universality, altruism, hope, cohesiveness, interpersonal learning, and others; no factor is universally largest or sufficient. Group purpose, composition, leadership, safety, culture, confidentiality limits, attendance, and phase affect process, and a therapy group is not equivalent to any task group.

items.title: Psychoanalytic Key Concepts
items.content: **Historical psychodynamic map:** Unconscious processes, conflict, defense, transference, countertransference, developmental experience, and recurring relationship patterns organize psychoanalytic formulations. Id, ego, superego, drives, and psychosexual stages are historical theoretical constructs, not directly observed brain systems or diagnostic facts. Contemporary psychodynamic therapies vary in focus and duration. Interpretation requires collaborative context and cannot infer childhood cause, hidden motive, or treatment need from one behavior.

items.title: Behavioral Activation
items.content: **Behavioral activation process:** Collaboratively monitor links among activities, context, mood, avoidance, and valued or reinforcing consequences; then test planned, feasible activities and problem-solve barriers. It is not simply telling a depressed person to stay busy or exercise, and immediate pleasure is not the only target. Risk assessment, functional analysis, pacing, disability and resource context, values, comorbidity, and outcome monitoring shape implementation.

items.title: Paradoxical Intention
items.content: **Paradoxical intention:** In selected formulations, a person deliberately approaches or exaggerates a feared response to alter anticipatory anxiety and the struggle to suppress it. Evidence is indication-specific, and the intervention is not a contest in which the therapist wins. It requires a clear collaborative rationale, consent, competence, risk assessment, cultural fit, and monitoring. Examples involving insomnia or anxiety are not self-treatment instructions and do not apply automatically to psychosis, suicidality, or every symptom.

items.title: Play Therapy
items.content: **Developmentally responsive medium:** Play therapy uses play, toys, stories, art, and relationship within a defined model to support communication and therapeutic work when verbal abstraction may be limited. Child-centered, cognitive-behavioral, filial, and other approaches differ. Play is not inherently diagnostic or curative, and symbolic meaning cannot be read from one act. Assessment, caregiver involvement, consent and assent, culture, safeguarding, competence, goals, and outcome monitoring matter.

items.title: Interpersonal Therapy (IPT)
items.content: **Time-limited interpersonal focus:** IPT links current depressive symptoms with one or more focal areas such as grief, role transitions, role disputes, or interpersonal deficits or sensitivities, using assessment, formulation, communication analysis, affect work, and role practice across phases. It is not generic advice to socialize and does not claim relationships are the sole cause of depression. Qualified assessment, risk management, adaptation, consent, and monitoring remain necessary.

items.title: Object Relations Therapy
items.content: **Historical object-relations framework:** Internalized representations of self and others, attachment, splitting, integration, and recurring relational expectations are formulated differently by Klein, Fairbairn, Winnicott, Kernberg, and later writers. An object is a representation of a person or relationship, not merely a physical object. These are theoretical constructs, not directly observed entities or diagnoses, and one relationship pattern cannot prove an early cause or dictate treatment.

items.title: ACT - Acceptance & Commitment Therapy
items.content: **Psychological flexibility:** ACT commonly organizes work around acceptance, cognitive defusion, present-moment awareness, self-as-context, values, and committed action. Acceptance means willing contact with experience in service of chosen action, not approval, resignation, or tolerating harm; defusion changes the relation to thoughts rather than proving them false. The hexaflex is a process map, not a six-step self-treatment protocol or guarantee of symptom reduction.

items.title: Bowen Family Systems Therapy
items.content: **Bowen theory cue:** Differentiation, triangles, family projection, multigenerational transmission, emotional cutoff, sibling position, and societal emotional process organize a systems formulation. items.title: Motivational Interviewing
items.content: **MI processes and spirit:** Partnership, acceptance, compassion, and evocation guide engaging, focusing, evoking, and planning. Open questions, affirmations, reflections, and summaries support conversation but are not MI by themselves. Change talk predicts or reflects movement probabilistically, while sustain talk is explored rather than confronted. MI does not manipulate, prescribe goals, or require immediate action; autonomy, discrepancy, culture, readiness, and safety remain central.

items.title: Rogers' Core Conditions
items.content: **Person-centered conditions with limits:** Rogers proposed psychological contact, client incongruence, therapist congruence, unconditional positive regard, empathic understanding, and the client's perception of the latter attitudes. UPR does not mean approving every action, empathy is not mind reading, and congruence is not unfiltered disclosure. The theory called the conditions necessary and sufficient under its terms; that historical claim is not a guarantee for every problem, client, setting, or outcome.

items.title: Paradoxical Interventions
items.content: **Model-specific paradox:** Strategic symptom prescription, scheduled symptoms, and Frankl's paradoxical intention use different rationales to disrupt maintaining patterns or anticipatory struggle. They do not guarantee control or symptom loss and are not tricks for defeating resistance. Use requires collaborative framing, consent, competence, risk screening, attention to coercion and culture, and close monitoring. Examples are not instructions for self-treatment or substitutes for emergency or disorder-specific care.

items.title: Existential Therapy
items.content: **Existential concerns as inquiry:** Death, freedom and responsibility, isolation, and meaninglessness are Yalom's organizing concerns; Frankl, May, Bugental, and others differ in emphasis. Existential anxiety is not automatically pathology or growth, and meaning is not prescribed by the therapist. The approach relies on phenomenological exploration and relationship rather than a fixed technique set. Safety, diagnosis, culture, spirituality, power, goals, and evidence-supported care remain relevant.

items.title: Gestalt Therapy Techniques
items.content: **Awareness-oriented experiments:** Empty-chair dialogue, exaggeration, reversal, present-centered inquiry, and attention to figure-ground or contact may deepen awareness when collaboratively chosen. They are not scripts, and changing pronouns or saying "I wont" can misrepresent constraint or blame a client. Unfinished business and contact-boundary terms are theoretical formulations. Consent, pacing, stability, culture, relationship, competence, and observed response govern use.

items.title: Cognitive Distortions - Beck
items.content: **Cognitive-therapy labels:** All-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization, selective attention, mind reading, fortune telling, personalization, labeling, emotional reasoning, magnification or minimization, and rigid should statements can organize collaborative examination of thoughts. A label is a hypothesis about a thought in context, not a diagnosis or proof that emotion is irrational. Therapy tests evidence, alternatives, function, behavior, and outcomes rather than replacing every negative thought with a positive one.
